title: Sheriffs defend work with ICE under immigration enforcement program
summary: Two days before the Senate hears a bill to ban local law enforcement agencies from entering into immigration enforcement agreements with federal officials, sheriffs gathered Tuesday in Annapolis to tell lawmakers to leave 287(g) agreements alone.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 20, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 20, 2026

Two days before a Maryland Senate committee hears a bill that would ban local law enforcement agencies from entering into immigration enforcement agreements with the federal government, some sheriffs gathered Tuesday in Annapolis to tell lawmakers to let them “do their job.”

Specifically, the sheriffs want to continue operating under 287(g) agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that let them hold suspects an additional 48 hours, if they are determined to be undocumented, to hand over to ICE for immigration proceedings.

“It’s a true public safety tool,” said Frederick County Sheriff Chuck Jenkins, who was backed by other sheriffs and Senate Republicans. “We simply don’t return criminals back onto the street. We hand those individuals off to ICE in a safe setting in their detention center.”

Besides Frederick County, which Jenkins said has had an agreement with ICE since 2008, seven other sheriff’s departments in the state have signed 287(g) agreements, five of them in the past year.

The sheriffs were in Annapolis to speak out against Senate Bill 245, which would prohibit a sheriff, local police or any “agent of the state” from entering into an agreement with the federal government to enforce civil immigration law. The fill, set to be heard Thursday by the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee, has some powerful sponsors: In addition to Sen. Karen Lewis Young (D-Frederick), the bill is being backed this year by the committee chair, Sen. William C. Smith Jr.  (D-Montgomery), and Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City).

In a meeting with reporters Tuesday, Ferguson said that “everyone is entitled to their opinion, but that he was “disappointed by the sentiment that sheriffs in Maryland feel that what is happening and the way that ICE is attempting to enforce law – anonymously with masks, indiscriminately ripping people out of cars and homes – I find it quite disappointing that that is the standard that offices want to partner with.”

“It gives me a great deal of pause about the efficacy of the trust between the populace that they serve and the future for law enforcement moving forward,” he said.

A ban on 287(g) agreements was included in an immigration bill in last year’s legislative session, but that language was stripped out at the last minute in the Senate. Criminal justice reform advocates have since pointed to the failure of that law as ICE tactics have become more aggressive in the past year under President Donald Trump (R). Data from the Prison Policy Initiative showed the more than 3,000 people in Maryland were arrested last year by ICE.

The federal agency has received intense scrutiny since the shooting of Renee Good, 37, in Minneapolis this month.

But Sen. William G. Folden (R-Frederick) said that what’s happening in Minnesota isn’t happening in Maryland. Claims that the 287(g) program isn’t working in Maryland represents “a lot of fear mongering. We hear a lot of distraction and virtue signaling.”

“Our sheriffs want to be very clear: We have no police … going out boots-on-the-ground, rounding people up and arresting illegal immigrants on the ground. That’s completely false,” he said. “Anybody that’s saying that is not familiar with Maryland’s laws and not familiar with the policies and the cooperative agreements with ICE.”

The immigrant rights group CASA has said the 287(g) program permits racial profiling, but the sheriffs say no.

When asked Tuesday if Black, Latino and other Marylanders of color should fear being detained by ICE, Harford County Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler had this message: “If you don’t want to get caught up in the 287(g) program, don’t sell drugs, don’t break the law, and you won’t get arrested and you won’t get screened in.”

Jenkins has said that if a ban on 287(g) is passed, it would be unconstitutional, a point he repeated Tuesday.

“The fact I’m a duly elected sheriff, I think there’s a real court challenge there,” Jenkins said. “I think sheriffs would prevail. I really do.”

— Maryland Matters reporter Danielle J. Brown contributed to this report.
